How safe vaccines are and why they protect us from serious illness
The flu jab gives you the flu or weakens your body.
The injected flu vaccine contains inactivated virus or only fragments of it, which cannot cause flu. It trains the immune system to recognise the real virus.
A vaccine is like a practice drill for your body. It does not make you ill; it teaches your body how to defend itself if it meets the disease.
World Health Organization and the Romanian Ministry of Health
“Silent” high blood pressure and preventing heart attacks
If I don't have a headache, my blood pressure must be fine.
High blood pressure often gives no sign until it harms the heart or blood vessels. That is why it needs measuring regularly.
High blood pressure is like an over-inflated hose: nothing hurts until it bursts. That is why it needs measuring often, even when you feel perfectly well.
How to bring a fever down safely and when to see a doctor
A child's high fever must be brought down straight away by rubbing on alcohol or vinegar.
Alcohol and vinegar are absorbed through a child's thin skin and can cause serious poisoning. Fever is treated with fever medicine dosed for the child's weight, and plenty of fluids.
Never put surgical spirit or vinegar on a child's skin: it poisons them through the skin. Give water or tea and the fever syrup your doctor recommends.
Why antibiotics don't cure viral infections, and what resistance means
Any bad cold clears up faster if you take an antibiotic from day one.
Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only act on bacteria. Taken needlessly, they upset the gut flora and encourage antibiotic resistance.
Antibiotics only kill bacteria, not the viruses that cause colds. If you take them for a cold, you upset your stomach and don't get better any faster.
“Prof. Dr. Matei Balș” National Institute for Infectious Diseases

Checking blood sugar with a meter
How to check your blood sugar correctly
When you test correctly, your doctor gets good numbers. You also see how food and movement change your blood sugar.
Wash your hands with warm water and plain soap. Dry them well with a clean towel. Warm water brings blood into your fingers.
Do not use rubbing alcohol or scented wet wipes. Alcohol dries the skin, and perfume or glycerine can spoil the result.
Do not prick a wet finger. Water thins the blood and the meter shows a lower number than the real one.
Get the meter and needle ready
Put a new strip into the meter until you hear a click or see the drop sign on the screen. Put a new needle (lancet) in the pricker and set it to depth 2 or 3.
Keep the strip box tightly closed, in a dry place, away from sun and heat.
Do not use the same needle more than once. A blunt needle hurts more and damages the skin.
Prick the side of your finger
Prick the side of your fingertip, not the middle. Gently rub the finger from base to tip until a round drop forms. Touch the drop with the end of the strip.
The sides have fewer nerves than the middle, so it hurts less.
Do not squeeze the finger hard. Tissue fluid comes out too, thins the blood and spoils the result.
Read, write down, throw away the needle
Wait 5 seconds for the number. Write it in a notebook or app, with the time and whether it was before or after a meal. Put the cap on the needle and throw it into a hard plastic bottle or box.
One number alone does not tell the whole story. Also write down what you ate, so you can talk it over with your doctor.
Do not throw uncapped needles in the normal rubbish. Someone could get pricked.
You are under 70 mg/dL and feel dizzy or cannot think clearly. Use the 15/15 rule.
You are often over 250 mg/dL and do not know which food caused it.
The meter often shows an error. Check the strips' expiry date or the battery.
How to protect your feet from wounds
Diabetes can make your feet numb. Then you do not feel pain or heat well. A small blister or cut can go unnoticed if you do not look every day.
Look at your soles every evening
Every evening, in good light, look closely at your soles, heels and between your toes. If you cannot lift your foot, put a mirror on the floor or ask someone in your family.
Look for redness, blisters, cracks or spots that feel warm.
Do not ignore a red spot or a callus and hope it goes away. With diabetes, wounds heal more slowly.
Wash and dry your feet well
Wash your feet every day with lukewarm water and mild soap. Do not soak them for more than 5 minutes, so the skin does not dry out. Pat them dry with a soft towel, especially between the toes.
Test the water with your elbow or a thermometer, not your foot. Your foot may not feel that the water is too hot.
Do not leave the skin damp between your toes. Fungus grows easily there.
Cream on the heels, not between toes
Put urea cream or a simple greasy cream on your heels, soles and the top of your foot. The skin stays soft and does not crack.
Germs get in through cracked skin. Using cream often keeps the skin whole.
Do not put cream between your toes. The skin there gets too soft and breaks.
Wear white or light cotton socks, with no thick seams and no tight elastic at the ankle. Before you put your shoes on, feel inside with your hand for small stones, folds or nails.
On white socks you see a small spot of blood or pus straight away.
Never walk barefoot, not even at home or on the beach. A splinter or a sharp bit can make a deep wound.
A wound, cut or blister has not healed after 48 hours.

Look for deep cracks and thick hard skin. Germs get in through cracks.

Damp skin here leads to athlete's foot. Keep it fully dry.
You press hardest here when you walk. If your foot is numb, a callus that does not hurt can hide a wound.
Tight shoes rub here and cause blisters and calluses. Choose shoes that are wide at the front.

Meal with lots of sugar and white flour
Sweets, sugary drinks and white bread push blood sugar up very fast. Then it drops just as fast, and you feel tired and hungry.
The pancreas has to release a lot of insulin quickly to bring blood sugar back to normal.
Meal with vegetables, protein and fiber
Vegetables, lean meat or eggs, and whole grains make sugar enter the blood more slowly. Your numbers stay good.
Fiber forms a kind of gel in the gut that slows sugar going into the blood.
A brisk 20–30 minute walk after a meal makes your muscles take sugar straight from the blood. The peak is much lower.
Working muscles take sugar from the blood even with little insulin. That is why the after-meal peak is lower.

Everyday habits that keep your heart and blood pressure healthy.
Your heart pumps blood around your body every minute of the day. Looking after it lowers your risk of heart disease and stroke. Most of the habits that help are small.
High blood pressure and cholesterol quietly strain your arteries and make your heart work harder for years without signs.
A healthy heart and normal blood pressure give you better stamina, steadier breathing and lower risk of stroke.
Using less salt, walking briskly most days and checking your blood pressure regularly protect your heart.
Walk briskly or do any activity you like. Short walks count too.
Eat more vegetables, fruit and whole grains. Use less salt and eat fewer ready-made foods.
Have your blood pressure and cholesterol checked. Problems are easier to treat when found early.

What raises your risk and how to keep your blood sugar steady.
Diabetes affects how your body handles sugar in the blood. Type 2 diabetes is often linked to daily habits. You can often delay or prevent it, and with the right help you can live well with it.
In type 2 diabetes, sugar stays in the blood instead of entering your cells, and can quietly harm blood vessels for years.
Keeping your blood sugar steady gives you even energy through the day and protects your eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.
Small daily habits like filling half your plate with vegetables and walking after meals lower your risk.

Cheap, simple food choices that keep you healthy.
Eating well does not have to be hard or expensive. A few simple rules, followed most days, give your body what it needs.
Fiber from vegetables and whole grains keeps your blood sugar and blood pressure steady.
Simple home-cooked food gives you steady energy through the day and prevents tiredness after meals.
Seasonal vegetables, beans and lentils are cheap, and drinking water instead of sugary drinks helps straight away.

Easy ways to move more, whatever your fitness.
Moving more is one of the best things you can do for your body and mind. You do not need a gym. Everyday movement counts.
Movement gets your blood flowing, strengthens your heart and muscles, and helps your cells use blood sugar for energy.
Moving regularly gives you steadier energy, deeper sleep at night, and better balance and mobility.
You do not need a gym: stand up every hour and take a 15–30 minute walk on most days.

Look after your mind and know when to ask for help.
Your mental health is part of your health. Everyone has good and bad times. Asking for help when you need it is normal.
Long-term stress keeps stress hormones high, tightening your muscles, raising your pulse and disturbing your sleep.
Looking after your mind helps you sleep better, focus during the day and stay connected with the people around you.
Slow breathing exercises, regular sleep hours and talking openly with someone you trust ease tension quickly.
Spend time with people you trust. Being close to others protects your mind.

Why quitting is worth it and what makes it easier.
Stopping smoking is one of the best things you can do for your health. Your body starts to recover quickly. Most people try several times before they stop for good.
Within hours of your last cigarette, oxygen levels rise, blood vessels relax and your lungs begin clearing themselves.
As your lungs and circulation recover, you breathe more easily on stairs, cough less and regain your sense of taste.
Setting a quit date, waiting out 3-minute cravings and asking your doctor for support double your chances of stopping.
Choose a day and tell people you trust. Plan what you will do when you want to smoke.
Stop-smoking services and approved aids make it more likely you stay smoke-free.
If you smoke again, do not give up. Learn from it and try again.

Tests that find health problems early, often before you feel ill.
Screening looks for early signs of illness before you notice anything wrong. Problems found early are often easier to treat.
Many conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes or early cancers start quietly in the body long before any pain appears.
Even when you feel well every day, a routine check gives you peace of mind and catches changes while treatment is simple.

Women's health needs change through life, from periods and pregnancy to menopause and after. Knowing what is normal for you helps you notice when something changes.
A woman's body goes through natural hormone shifts from menstruation and pregnancy to menopause, affecting bones, heart and mood.
Knowing what is normal for your body helps you spot breast changes, unusual bleeding or persistent pelvic pain early.
Regular cervical screening, monthly breast self-checks and routine pregnancy visits find problems early when they are easiest to treat.

The flu vaccine gives you the flu.

Many people think this because they feel a bit unwell soon after the vaccine. The vaccine contains inactive parts of the virus, which cannot cause the illness. It only teaches your body to fight the real virus.
You only get diabetes if you eat too much sugar.
Too much sugar can make you put on weight. But type 2 diabetes has several causes: your genes, not moving enough and how your body uses insulin. Sweets alone do not cause it.
If you have high blood pressure, you always get headaches or feel dizzy.
Most of the time, high blood pressure causes no signs at all. That is why it is called the silent killer. The only sure way to find it is to measure it regularly.
Antibiotics help you get over a cold or flu faster.

Colds and flu are caused by viruses. Antibiotics only work against bacteria. If you take them without a prescription, they harm the good bacteria in your gut. Over time, antibiotics also stop working as well.
If you can't feel a lump in your breast, you don't need a check-up.
A mammogram or breast ultrasound can find very small changes long before you can feel them. When a problem is found early, treatment is simpler and works better.
Filter cigarettes or heated tobacco don't harm your heart.
Nicotine and what you breathe in narrow your blood vessels and speed up your pulse, however you smoke. Quitting is the best thing you can do for your heart.
Pink Himalayan salt or sea salt is healthy, so you can eat as much as you like.

All kitchen salt is about 98% sodium chloride. Every kind raises blood pressure in the same way. Pink salt does not protect your heart any better than ordinary salt. What matters is the total: less than 5 grams a day.
Exercise only helps your health if you go to the gym or work out intensely.
Walking fast, gardening or taking the stairs all protect your heart. Every minute you move each day helps lower your blood pressure and blood sugar. You don't need expensive equipment.

If you have anxiety or feel sad for a long time, it means you are weak.

Anxiety and depression are real illnesses. They are shaped by the brain, hormones and stress in your life. They are not a weakness of character. Help from a specialist and guided breathing exercises help a lot.
All parts of your body work together. When you look after your blood vessels and organs, your whole body works more easily.
How it affects your daily life
Many health problems do not hurt at first. If you find them early, you keep your strength for work and family.
Small habits, done every day, help a lot over time. For example, a little movement and less salty food.

RediHealth helps you understand your health, find medical help and reach health workers who can help you.
We made RediHealth so you know what to do when you have a health worry. You can check your symptoms, read about an illness, or ask a doctor or a health mediator for help.

You feel that not enough air gets into your chest, especially when you move or lie down.
You feel everything is spinning around you, or you lose your balance when you stand up.
A little blood is taken from your finger or arm. The result shows the doctor what is happening in your body.
The 9 months when the baby grows in the mother's belly, until birth.
A small injection. It teaches the body, in children and adults, to defend itself against serious illness.
Someone's life is in danger. Call 112 now.
Measured in the morning, after at least 8 hours without food. It shows how much sugar is in your blood while your body rests.
Normal: 70–99 mg/dL. 100 to 125 mg/dL means prediabetes. 126 mg/dL or more on 2 tests can mean diabetes.
Fasting blood sugar. On test results it is called fasting plasma glucose. Normal is between 70 and 99 milligrams per deciliter.
Blood sugar 2 hours after a meal
Measured 2 hours after you start eating. It shows how well your body handles the sugar from food.
Normal: under 140 mg/dL. 140 to 199 mg/dL means your body struggles with sugar (impaired glucose tolerance). 200 mg/dL or more can mean diabetes.
Blood sugar 2 hours after a meal. Doctors call it postprandial glucose. Normal is under 140 milligrams per deciliter.
Your blood pushes too hard against the walls of your blood vessels, all the time. Your heart gets tired and the vessels get damaged.
Diagnosed when readings stay at 140/90 mmHg or higher. It is the biggest risk factor for heart attack and stroke.
High blood pressure. Doctors call it arterial hypertension. Above 140 over 90, your heart works too hard, even if nothing hurts.
Your blood pressure is lower than normal. You may feel dizzy when you stand up fast, see blurry, or faint.
Below 90/60 mmHg. If you feel fine, it can be normal for you. If you feel dizzy or faint, your doctor checks your fluids and salts (electrolytes).
Low blood pressure. Doctors call it arterial hypotension. Below 90 over 60, you may feel dizzy or weak when you stand up fast.
A clot fully blocks an artery of the heart. Part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen and starts to get damaged.
Emergency. Call 112. The artery must be opened in hospital (angioplasty) within the first hours.
Heart attack. Doctors call it acute myocardial infarction. If you feel crushing pain in your chest that spreads to your arm or jaw, call 112 now.
Blood suddenly stops reaching part of the brain, because of a clot or bleeding. Brain cells in that part die.
Emergency. Call 112. Doctors check the signs with the FAST test. The medicine that dissolves the clot (thrombolysis) is given within the first 4.5 hours.
Stroke. Doctors call it a cerebrovascular accident. If the face droops, an arm goes weak or speech is slurred, call 112 now.
Short of breath when active or lying down
You feel like you are choking or cannot breathe well. If it happens with light effort or lying flat in bed, your heart may be struggling.
Getting out of breath with effort, or needing several pillows to sleep (orthopnea), can mean fluid in the lungs (pulmonary congestion). See a cardiologist urgently.
Shortness of breath. Doctors call it dyspnea. If you struggle to breathe with light effort or when lying flat, see a doctor urgently.
Fluid collects in your ankles and lower legs. It happens when your heart or veins struggle to push blood back up.
If pressing with a finger leaves a dent (pitting), your body is holding on to water and salt. This is common in heart failure.
Swollen ankles and legs. Doctors call it peripheral edema. Water building up at the ankles often means your heart needs a doctor's care.
A blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the last 90 days. It shows how well your diabetes is controlled.
For most adults with diabetes, the target is under 7%. Above 8%, your doctor needs to review your treatment.
Average blood sugar over 3 months. On test results it is called HbA1c. For most people with diabetes, the target is under 7 percent.
Your heart beats fast and out of rhythm. Blood does not fully leave the upper chambers of the heart, so clots can form.
It makes a stroke 5 times more likely. You need blood-thinning tablets (anticoagulants) from a cardiologist.
Fast, irregular heartbeat. Doctors call it atrial fibrillation. See a cardiologist to prevent blood clots and stroke.
Your heart slowly loses the strength to pump enough blood to your organs. You tire quickly and fluid builds up in your body.
A long-term condition that gets worse over time. Weigh yourself every day, eat less than 5 g of salt a day and take your medicines exactly as prescribed.
Weak heart. Doctors call it chronic heart failure. Weigh yourself every day, eat little salt and take your medicines exactly as prescribed.
Numbness and tingling in the feet
High blood sugar damages the nerves in your feet. You feel pain less, so wounds can go unnoticed.
Common in people with diabetes. Look at the soles of your feet every day to spot wounds early.
Numbness and tingling in the feet. Doctors call it diabetic neuropathy. Check your feet every day to catch wounds early.
Years of high blood sugar damage the small blood vessels at the back of your eye (the retina).
A leading cause of preventable blindness in adults. Prevent it with an eye exam every year, with drops to widen your pupils, and an HbA1c under 7%.
Eye damage from diabetes. Doctors call it diabetic retinopathy. An eye exam every year protects your sight.
Dangerous acid build-up in the blood
When your body is badly short of insulin, it burns fat for energy. This makes poisonous acids (ketones) build up in your blood.
Life-threatening emergency. Signs: breath that smells fruity, vomiting that does not stop, confusion and dehydration.
Dangerous acid build-up in the blood. Doctors call it diabetic ketoacidosis. If you are vomiting, confused or breathing fast, call 112.
A quick test that does not hurt. Small sensors go on your skin, and a machine records on paper how your heart beats.
Shows an irregular heartbeat, a heart that does not get enough blood (ischemia), and signs of a recent or old heart attack.
Heart rhythm test. Doctors call it an electrocardiogram, or ECG. It is quick, does not hurt and shows how your heart beats.
An ultrasound scan. On the screen you see the heart walls, how the valves move and how strongly the heart pumps.
Measures how much blood the heart pushes out with each beat (ejection fraction, LVEF). It also finds valve problems and a thickened heart muscle.
Ultrasound of the heart. Doctors call it an echocardiogram. It shows how the valves move and how strongly the heart pumps.
A device with a cuff that goes on your arm. It inflates by itself and shows your blood pressure and pulse.
Good for checking at home. Choose a clinically tested model with an upper-arm cuff, not a wrist one.
Automatic blood pressure monitor. Models with an upper-arm cuff give the most accurate readings at home.
A small device. Put a drop of blood from the side of your fingertip on a strip, and it shows your blood sugar in a few seconds.
Helps you keep track of your diabetes yourself. You need test strips that fit your meter and sterile single-use needles (lancets).
Blood sugar meter, or glucometer. It shows your blood sugar from 1 drop of blood in a few seconds.
The form your family doctor gives you. If you are insured, it makes your specialist visit free or partly paid by national health insurance.
Valid for 30 days for a sudden illness, and up to 90 days for long-term illnesses followed in national health programmes.
Referral to a specialist. With it, national health insurance pays all or part of your specialist visits and tests.

Discounted or free prescription. Treatment for diabetes and other long-term illnesses is paid for by public health insurance.

The hospital department that is open day and night, 24 hours a day. Serious cases are treated here.

How to measure your blood pressure at home
For 30 minutes before, skip coffee, smoking and exercise. Go to the toilet. Then sit quietly in a chair for 5 minutes without talking.
A full bladder or a lively chat can push your reading up by 10–15 mmHg.
Do not measure right after climbing stairs, carrying heavy bags or an argument.
Sit on a chair with a backrest, back straight, feet flat on the floor. Rest your arm on a table. The middle of the cuff should be level with your heart.
If your arm hangs down by your side, the monitor shows a higher number than your real one.
Do not cross your legs. It squeezes the veins and raises your blood pressure.
Put the cuff on bare skin
Put the cuff straight on your skin, 2–3 cm above the elbow. The tube should run down the middle of your arm. Fasten it so one finger fits underneath.
Use a clinically tested upper-arm monitor, not a wrist one.
Do not roll up a tight sleeve that squeezes your arm. Never put the cuff over thick clothes.
Measure twice and write it down
Start the monitor. Stay still and quiet until the cuff goes down. Wait 1–2 minutes and measure again. Write down both readings and your pulse.
The first reading is often a bit higher because you are tense. The second one shows your real pressure better.
Never take an extra dose of your medicine after one high reading. Ask your doctor first.
